tiles.title: Bar Charts and Histograms
tiles.summary: Learn to compare categories with plt.bar() and reveal distributions with plt.hist(), understanding the zero-baseline rule and the bins parameter.

steps.title: Comparing Cities with a Bar Chart
steps.lede: When you want to compare a number across discrete categories, a bar chart aligns every bar to a shared baseline so the eye can judge lengths at a glance.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to compare average delivery time across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano. A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups — which fits this comparison exactly.

`plt.bar(x, height)` (or `ax.bar(x, height)`) makes a bar plot with bars positioned at the given x coordinates and given heights, with the baseline defaulting to 0. Categorical names can be passed directly as the x argument: `plt.bar(city_avg.index, city_avg)` plots the three city names as bar positions and each city's average delivery time as the bar height.

before.code:
# Delivery times as a raw list — hard to compare cities
print(orders['delivery_time_minutes'].tolist())

annotations.text: A flat list gives no per-city comparison
groupby + mean produces one average per city
plt.bar(city_avg.index, city_avg) passes city names as x and averages as heights

blocks.change_summary: Adding groupby + plt.bar turns a flat list into a per-city comparison chart.

steps.title: Bar Charts: Live Code and the Zero-Baseline Rule
Why the Baseline Must Start at Zero
steps.lede: The bar chart's power comes from comparing lengths — and that only works when every bar starts at the same point.

blocks.text: Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye is good at comparing lengths when the objects being compared are aligned to a common baseline. Every bar starts at 0, so a taller bar genuinely represents a larger value — Kano's bar looks taller than Lagos's because its average delivery time is higher.

Starting bars at a value other than 0 — say 20 minutes — distorts the comparison. If Kano averages 30 minutes and Lagos 25, bars starting at 20 are 10 and 5 units tall: Kano's bar looks twice as long even though its average is only 5 minutes higher. Keep the baseline at 0.

steps.title: Seeing the Distribution with a Histogram
steps.lede: A histogram bins a numeric variable and draws one bar per bin — revealing the shape of the distribution rather than individual values.

blocks.text: A bar chart compares categories, but delivery times are a numeric variable. You might instead want to see how those times are distributed — how many deliveries were fast, how many were slow, and whether most cluster in the middle. A histogram answers that question.

`plt.hist(x, bins=...)` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars. `plt.hist(orders['delivery_time_minutes'])` bins every delivery time and shows how many orders fall into each time range.

The `bins` parameter defaults to `rcParams['hist.bins']`, which defaults to 10. Passing an integer sets that many equal-width bins; passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges; passing a string such as `'auto'` selects a binning strategy automatically.

before.code:
# Delivery times as a sorted list — shape is not visible
print(sorted(orders['delivery_time_minutes'].tolist()))

annotations.text: A sorted list shows individual values but not the distribution shape
plt.hist bins the values and draws one bar per bin, revealing the distribution shape

blocks.change_summary: plt.hist() replaces a sorted list with a binned bar chart that reveals the distribution shape.

steps.title: Bar Charts and Histograms: What You Learned
steps.lede: Two chart types, two different questions — categories versus distribution.

blocks.text: Use `plt.bar(x, height)` to compare a numeric value across discrete categories, keeping the baseline at 0 so bar lengths stay honest. Use `plt.hist(x, bins=...)` to reveal how a numeric variable is distributed — it bins the values and draws one bar per bin.

remediation_steps.title: Bar Charts Are for Categories
remediation_steps.lede: A bar chart compares a numeric value across discrete groups — not distributions or trends.

blocks.text: A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups. The three cities Lagos, Abuja, and Kano are discrete categories, so a bar chart comparing their average delivery times is the right fit. A histogram would show the spread of times, not a city-by-city comparison.

remediation_steps.title: The Baseline Must Be Zero
remediation_steps.lede: Shifting the baseline away from zero makes bars misleading because the eye compares lengths.

blocks.text: Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye compares lengths from a common baseline. If Kano averages 30 minutes and Lagos 25, bars starting at 20 are 10 and 5 units tall — Kano's bar looks twice as long even though its average is only 5 minutes higher. Keep the baseline at 0 so lengths stay proportional to values.

remediation_steps.title: How plt.hist() Bins Your Data
remediation_steps.lede: plt.hist() doesn't just count values — it groups them into bins first.

blocks.text: `plt.hist(x, bins=...)` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars. Each bar represents a range of values, not a single value — that's what makes a histogram different from a bar chart.

remediation_steps.title: Controlling Bins in plt.hist()
remediation_steps.lede: The bins parameter accepts an integer, a sequence, or a strategy string.

blocks.text: The `bins` parameter defaults to `rcParams['hist.bins']`, which defaults to 10. Passing an integer sets that many equal-width bins. Passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges. Passing a string such as `'auto'` selects a binning strategy automatically.

tiles.title: Line Plots, Scatter Plots, and Box Plots
tiles.summary: Plot trends over time with plt.plot(), relationships between two numeric variables with plt.scatter(), and per-group distributions with plt.boxplot().

steps.title: Tracking Trends Over Time with a Line Plot
steps.lede: A line plot connects measured points in order — making rises and falls in the data immediately visible.

blocks.text: Suppose you have this week's average Lagos delivery time for each of 5 days and want to see whether it is getting better or worse. Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other.
A line graph plots the measured points and then draws a line that connects those points, making it easier to see how the values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time.

`plt.plot(x, y)` plots the y-values against the given x-values. `plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [21, 23, 19, 25, 20])` plots 5 days of average Lagos delivery times, with the connecting line making the day-to-day rise and fall immediately readable.

steps.title: Exploring Relationships with a Scatter Plot
steps.lede: A scatter plot places one point per (x, y) pair — making the relationship between two numeric variables visible at a glance.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to see whether delivery distance and delivery time move together across your orders. A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted simultaneously along the horizontal and vertical axis, and is useful for focusing on the relationship between two series.

`plt.scatter(x, y)` (or `ax.scatter(x, y)`) makes a scatter plot of the y-values against the x-values, one point per (x, y) pair. `plt.scatter(orders['distance_km'], orders['delivery_time_minutes'])` plots one point per order, with distance on the x-axis and delivery time on the y-axis.

steps.title: Reading a Box Plot
steps.lede: Every part of a box plot has a name — learn to read the box, whiskers, and flier points.

blocks.text: Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side — showing spread, median, and outliers in a single compact shape.

blocks.title: Box Plot Anatomy

nodes.label: Upper whisker — farthest point within 1.5×IQR above Q3
Q3 (third quartile) — top edge of box
Q1 (first quartile) — bottom edge of box
Lower whisker — farthest point within 1.5×IQR below Q1

blocks.alt_text: A layered diagram of box plot anatomy from top to bottom: flier point (outlier) above the upper whisker; upper whisker reaching to the farthest in-range point above Q3; Q3 at the top of the box; median as a line inside the box; Q1 at the bottom of the box; lower whisker reaching to the farthest in-range point below Q1.

steps.title: The Box, Whiskers, and Flier Points
steps.lede: The box spans Q1 to Q3; whiskers reach 1.5×IQR beyond the box; anything further is a flier.

blocks.text: `plt.boxplot(x)` (or `ax.boxplot(x)`) draws a box plot from the data in x; it accepts array-like data and can draw one or more boxes. The box extends from Q1 to Q3, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend to the farthest data point lying within 1.5× the IQR from the box; points past the whisker ends are flier points (outliers).

If Lagos's box runs from Q1 = 20 to Q3 = 30 minutes, the IQR is 10 minutes. The whiskers can reach at most 1.5 × 10 = 15 minutes beyond the box — no lower than 5 minutes and no higher than 45 minutes — so a 50-minute Lagos delivery would be drawn as a separate flier point.

steps.title: Box Plots: Distribution and Outliers
Comparing Multiple Cities Side by Side
steps.lede: Pass a sequence of arrays to draw one box per group, and use tick_labels to name each box.

blocks.text: Passing a sequence of 1D arrays as x draws one box for each array in the sequence; `tick_labels=[...]` labels each boxplot's tick accordingly instead of leaving it as a numeric value. `plt.boxplot([lagos_times, abuja_times, kano_times], tick_labels=['Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'])` draws three boxes side by side, each labeled with its city name.

steps.title: Line, Scatter, and Box Plots: What You Learned
steps.lede: Three chart types for three different questions about numeric data.

blocks.text: Use `plt.plot(x, y)` to show how a value changes over time. Use `plt.scatter(x, y)` to explore the relationship between two numeric variables. Use `plt.boxplot(x)` to compare the full spread — median, quartiles, and outliers — across multiple groups.

remediation_steps.title: The Connecting Line Reveals the Trend
remediation_steps.lede: Without the line, you see points; with it, you see the direction of change.

blocks.text: A line graph plots the measured points and then draws a line that connects those points, making it easier to see how the values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time. The line between day 2 (23 min) and day 3 (19 min) slopes downward — showing improvement — in a way that a list of numbers does not.

remediation_steps.title: Scatter Plots Show Relationships Between Two Variables
remediation_steps.lede: Each point encodes one (x, y) pair — the pattern of points reveals whether the two variables move together.

blocks.text: A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted simultaneously along the horizontal and vertical axis. `plt.scatter(orders['distance_km'], orders['delivery_time_minutes'])` places one point per order — if longer distances consistently produce longer times, the points will trend upward from left to right.

remediation_steps.title: The Box Spans Q1 to Q3
remediation_steps.lede: The box edges mark the first and third quartiles; the line inside marks the median.

blocks.text: The box extends from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3) of the data, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend to the farthest data point lying within 1.5× the IQR from the box; points past the whisker ends are flier points (outliers).

remediation_steps.title: Box Plots Compare Distributions, Not Just Averages
remediation_steps.lede: A box plot shows spread, median, and outliers — a bar chart shows only a single summary value per group.

blocks.text: Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side. Unlike a bar chart that shows only the average per city, a box plot shows how spread out the delivery times are, where the middle half falls, and whether any deliveries are unusually slow.
